# January–February faculty research, with a December check
Research packet for Mark and the other seats. Source priority: university/faculty pages, original papers, and project pages. Bios are the institutions’ published accounts; I treat them as leads, not independent verification of every career claim.

## January 16 — security and privacy
Speakers: **Charnon Pattiyanon** and **Natnatee Dokmai**. The scheduled topic is “What You Can Safely Put Into an AI Tool,” followed by audience project Q&A. Event page: https://cmkl.ac.th/news-events/ai-inspiration-security-and-privacy

### Charnon Pattiyanon — AI systems, software/security engineering
- CMKL lists his AI interests as distributed training and inference, distributed resource management, NLP, LLMs, speech recognition, GANs, and object detection. His broader work includes software engineering, formal methods, information security/privacy, identity/access management, and decentralized identity.
- A recent item on his own publication page is **“LLM-Assisted Property Verification for Auditing Solidity Smart Contract Security using GraphCodeBERT and Graph Neural Networks”** (InCIT 2026, Bangkok). That makes the model role an audit/screening component for software properties, not a general-purpose chatbot claim. The published listing says accepted; the full proceedings/independent performance assessment were not available in the sources I checked.
- Other listed work covers compliance properties for self-sovereign identity, detecting weaknesses in SSI with domain-specific models and knowledge graphs, human-centered medical-staff scheduling, OCR, and physics-informed models for PM2.5 / fire-source attribution in Thailand. This is a broader practical engineering-and-governance portfolio.
- CMKL’s profile reports earlier technical-lead/senior-engineer work at Thai company G-Able implementing identity and access management, and current teaching/IT leadership at CMKL. I found no reason to describe G-Able as a current affiliation.
- Sources: https://cmkl.ac.th/faculty-staff-person-details/charnon-pattiyanon · https://chnpat.github.io/publication.html

**Why this might matter to our work:** the strongest fit is secure LLM use, distributed/local inference, identity boundaries, auditability, and testing whether a model-assisted system reliably checks something. For a small, public-safe demonstration, we could show a local model answering from a deliberately tiny, non-sensitive source packet and ask how to test refusal, provenance, and unsafe outputs. A Puppy/Puppf system-security angle is possible; an island/Project-Spiral angle is about controlled agent interactions and evidence trails. Those are useful questions, not a claim that his published research is about our project.

### Natnatee Dokmai — privacy-preserving computation for sensitive data
- CMKL lists cryptography, security/privacy, bioinformatics, trusted execution environments (TEEs), and biomedical/genomic data science. His faculty bio reports a PhD in Computer Science from Indiana University, postdoctoral work at Yale School of Medicine, and a visiting graduate student/postdoctoral role at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. The MIT/Broad connection is real in the profile; do not shorten that to “MIT professor.”
- In **“Privacy-preserving genotype imputation in a trusted execution environment”** (Cell Systems, 2021), the team built SMac to process private genomes inside Intel SGX, with attention to side-channel attacks, scalability, and accuracy. The paper makes clear that simply uploading sensitive data to a remote service blocks access for some researchers.
- In **“Secure phasing of private genomes … with TX-Phase”** (Genome Research, 2025), the team extends the idea to secure haplotype phasing. The methods include data-oblivious algorithms, compressed reference panels, and fixed-point arithmetic to reduce side-channel leakage while retaining usable runtime. The work has Yale, UCSD, and NIH/NCI affiliations; his profile also reports Broad/Harvard ties.
- Sources: https://www.cmkl.ac.th/meet-faculty/natnatee-dokmai · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34450045/ · https://genome.cshlp.org/content/35/12/2626 · code: https://github.com/hcholab/txphase

**Why this might matter to our work:** this is the most direct research fit for private/local AI, but it is specifically secure computation for genomics—not a claim that a local model is automatically private. A useful conversation would ask for a threat-model checklist for an offline model or agent: what can leak through logs, memory, updates, and the host machine; when a TEE adds protection; and what local-only does and does not guarantee. The Project-Spiral island link is indirect but promising as a data-governance question: which interaction traces are retained, who can attribute them, and how do we label observation versus inference? Keep all demo data synthetic/public; no genomic or personal data.

## February 20 — medical AI and imaging
Speakers: **Sarun Gulyanon** and **Antoine Merlet**. Event: “The Future of AI in the Healthcare System,” with project Q&A. Event page: https://cmkl.ac.th/news-events/ai-inspiration-saturday-medical

### Sarun Gulyanon — computer vision, biomedical imaging, and signal/data analysis
- CMKL reports a PhD in Computer Science from Purdue, with doctoral work on neuron morphology in microscopy images. His current interests include machine learning, computer vision, biomedical imaging, data science, NLP, and signal processing.
- His work spans more than hospital images. Examples include **VISHIEN-MAAT**, a scrollytelling explanation of how a Siamese neural network performs visual similarity matching; an autoencoder approach to reconstruct noisy/low-quality FTIR and Raman spectra in microplastic analysis; and more recent work on classifying microplastic types from filter-interfered FTIR spectra using dimensionality reduction and deep learning.
- The first example is unusually relevant to explaining an AI system to a nontechnical audience; the spectra work is a concrete example of handling messy real-world inputs rather than assuming clean data. His profile lists Thai university and research collaborations; I found no specific current commercial affiliation to report.
- Sources: https://www.cmkl.ac.th/faculty-staff-person-details/sarun-gulyanon · https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03288 · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8674871/ · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40819467/

**Why this might matter to our work:** if we want to show the island or local model to visitors, his explainability work suggests a better conversation than “look, the model is smart”: what visual evidence lets a newcomer understand the behavior? His signal work might also help if we ever have noisy camera/audio/sensor inputs. This is an interface/evaluation analogy; his cited projects are not agent-island research, and I would not bring a medical dataset.

### Antoine Merlet — PET/CT imaging, simulation, and validation
- CMKL’s profile describes a PhD in computer engineering/automation/signal processing and a master’s in medical imaging. His interests include deep learning, classification, segmentation, registration, and computer-aided diagnosis across PET/CT/SPECT/MRI.
- A concrete paper is **“Validation of a Discovery MI 4-ring model…”** (EJNMMI Physics, 2024). It combines a GATE Monte Carlo simulator with a clinical PET reconstruction package and compares simulations to measured scanner results using NEMA NU 2-2018 tests. The paper reports good agreement in several ranges, but also names limits (for example, less accurate high-activity behavior and spatial-blurring differences). This is useful practice in stating where a simulation stops matching reality.
- His profile reports collaboration with the University of Burgundy’s chemistry institute, Georges-François Leclerc Cancer Center, and GE HealthCare during PET/CT doctoral work. That is a research-collaboration history, not evidence of a current GE role or endorsement.
- Sources: https://cmkl.ac.th/meet-faculty/antoine-merlet · https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40658-024-00616-4

**Why this might matter to our work:** methodologically, this is a strong fit for any simulation or synthetic-data claim: define a real reference, compare outputs, report the residual error, and state the regime where the model fails. That could inform how we validate agent-island runs or Puppf test fixtures; the application domains are otherwise distinct. A sensible question is how to distinguish “the simulator agrees on the measured quantities” from “the simulator is a complete substitute for the real system.”

## December 11 — José Moura and the SPIRAL connection
CMKL lists José Moura (CMU) as keynote speaker at the AI Engineering & Innovation Summit, 9:00–17:00 at SCBX NEXT TECH, Siam Paragon. The talk is “AI Then, Now, and Beyond.” https://www.cmkl.ac.th/news-events/ai-has-come-a-long-way-how-much-further-can-it-go

The connection Mark flagged is unusually legible:
- Moura earned MS, EE, and DSc degrees at MIT; he is now a CMU University Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering, with a courtesy Biomedical Engineering appointment.
- He is one of the named SPIRAL project authors/leaders. CMU’s SPIRAL project automatically generates platform-tuned high-performance implementations of DSP algorithms; it combines signal processing/AI with compilers and computer architecture. It is also open-source and has a commercial-support route through SpiralGen. This is a genuine **name collision** with Mark’s Project-Spiral, plus shared interest in AI/automation and systems. The actual research topics are different: code generation and numerical kernels versus our small multi-agent island.
- Moura’s wider work includes graph signal processing, machine learning, signal/image/video processing, and distributed detection/inference in networks.
- Sources: https://ece.cmu.edu/directory/bios/moura-jose.html · https://www.spiral.net/ · https://users.ece.cmu.edu/~moura/research.html

**December assessment:** enough for a brief, friendly question at the summit, not enough to pitch a collaboration or claim a scientific match. The same-name opener can be honest and fun: “I found CMU’s SPIRAL while researching your talk. My Project-Spiral is a tiny multi-agent island, so it’s a completely different use of the name. I’m interested in how you think about automation and evaluation across very different AI systems.” If he’s available, ask about one point from the keynote; do not lead with an implied MIT or SPIRAL affiliation. No contact or registration has been made.

- **Local AI / Puppf / model operations:** Charnon (inference/security) + Natnatee (threat models and privacy limits).

- **Medical AI:** Sarun and Merlet can explain how imaging tasks differ from text/chat models. Do not imply our AI work is clinical.
- **MIT and systems:** Natnatee’s Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard history, and Moura’s MIT degrees, are traceable public background. These are interesting routes for introductions, not proof of a direct institutional invitation.
